entities.name: Jakob Salomon Bartholdy
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jakob Ludwig Salomon Bartholdy (1779–1825) was a pivotal Prussian diplomat and an influential patron of the arts, whose life bridged the late Enlightenment and early Romantic eras in Central Europe and Italy. Born into a prominent Jewish family in Berlin, he later converted to Christianity, adopting the surname Bartholdy, a decision reflecting the complex social and religious currents of his time. His significance in world history stems from his dual role as a state representative navigating the post-Napoleonic European order and as a central figure in the Roman art scene, where he championed the nascent Nazarene movement, thereby shaping the trajectory of German Romantic painting. His diplomatic postings, particularly as Prussian Consul General in Rome, provided the ideal nexus for his political duties and his profound engagement with art, culture, and intellectual exchange.

Bartholdy's early life saw him study law and philosophy before embarking on a diplomatic career that took him to Vienna and ultimately to Rome. Between 1805 and 1815, he resided in Rome, cultivating relationships with a circle of German Romantic artists, including Peter von Cornelius, Friedrich Overbeck, Philipp Veit, and Wilhelm von Schadow. These artists, rejecting academic classicism, sought inspiration in early Italian Renaissance and German medieval art, forming the 'Brotherhood of St. Luke' or Nazarenes. Bartholdy commissioned a series of frescoes for his Roman residence, the Casa Bartholdy, depicting the biblical story of Joseph and his brothers, executed between 1816 and 1817 by these leading Nazarene painters. This project served as a foundational showcase for their aesthetic principles, demonstrating a return to purity of line and sincere religious sentiment in art.
